lead: Parker is one of the newest towns on the Front Range, and most of its homes are under 25 years old. Hail, shifting clay soil and leaks in finished basements cause most of its water damage.
risk: hail damage, expansive soil and basement leaks
why: The median Parker home was built in 2004, and almost all were built after 1980. Many have basements, and owners often finish them years later. That puts carpet, drywall and furniture right where water collects first. A failed water heater, a cracked supply line or a window well that fills in a storm can soak a finished basement in minutes. Sprinkler lines and outdoor faucets also split in early freezes.

Douglas County sits on expansive clay that swells when wet and shrinks when dry. As the ground moves, foundations crack and water finds its way in after heavy rain or snowmelt. Hail is the other big risk. Parker sits in one of the busiest hail areas in the country, and summer storms crack shingles and dent gutters. The leaks often show up weeks later in the next rain.
image_alt: Worker on a ladder plastering a wall in an empty room
image_caption: Finished Parker basements are dried first, then patched and refinished.
problems: Homes across Parker after summer storms
tips: Blow out sprinkler lines before the first hard freeze.
Get the roof checked after any hail, even with no leak yet.
Keep window well covers on and wells free of debris.
Water the soil around the foundation evenly in dry spells.
areas: Calls come from Stonegate, Stroh Ranch, Pradera, Idyllwilde, Clarke Farms, Canterberry Crossing and Downtown Parker, plus Castle Pines, Lone Tree and Franktown.

faq.q: Why does my Parker basement get wet with no plumbing leak?
faq.a: The usual causes are foundation cracks, window wells that fill with water, or downspouts that dump water too close to the house. Parker's clay soil swells when wet and presses on basement walls. Extend downspouts, check the grading and seal cracks. DryFlare can dry the space when water gets in.
